1c3af95d5a:
This is the second half of objective 2.3. Chapter 05 covered the request and response contract of the Messages API. This chapter covers five things around it:

  • how output leaves the model incrementally: streaming events, and how to accumulate them;
  • how non-text input gets in: images, PDFs, the Files API;
  • how answers point back at their sources: citations and search-result blocks;
  • how enterprise data reaches a stateless API: stuffing vs retrieval vs tools;
  • what changes when the same API is consumed through Amazon Bedrock or Google Vertex AI: model IDs, auth, feature lag.

The story runs from chunked HTTP and Server-Sent Events to multimodal models and cloud marketplaces. Implementations are in Python and Java.
b589d3de6c: Neighbouring chapters: chapter 05 (requests, responses, stop reasons, errors, rate limits), chapter 07 (Batch API, and realtime vs batch), chapter 14 (SDKs as REST wrappers, raw SSE on the wire, websockets) and chapter 15 (prompt caching and cost). This chapter points to them rather than repeating them.
42a4494758:
The Messages API is one stateless function, but the shape of what flows through it varies: output can arrive all at once or as a stream of typed events that your code must accumulate, and input can be text, images, PDFs or references to uploaded files, optionally marked so the answer cites exact passages.

Around that function sit two architecture decisions that the exam tests by scenario: how your data gets into each request (put it all in, retrieve the relevant part, or let the model fetch it with tools), and which platform serves the call (Anthropic directly, Bedrock or Vertex), which changes authentication, model names and which features exist, but not the request body.
262eab913d:
Everything in the chapter hangs off those two sentences.

Streaming changes how the response is delivered, not what the model does. It's the same tokens, the same cost, the same stop reasons, delivered as a sequence of events so a person can start reading before generation ends.

Images and PDFs are content blocks, like text. The API converts them into the same token space, so they cost tokens and sit in the context window like everything else. The Files API is a storage service: upload bytes once, and refer to them by ID. Citations make the model's grounding inspectable.

None of these changes the core contract from chapter 05. Each one adds one kind of block or event to it.
ec8d22a7a7:
The data-access decision is older than LLMs, and the platform decision is a familiar enterprise one. But both take specific forms here. A 40-page plan catalogue and a 30,000-article knowledge base need different patterns. A customer's open orders need a third. A bank or carrier that buys all its cloud through AWS will consume Claude through Bedrock. Its developers must know that the Files API, URL image sources and the Message Batches endpoint aren't there.

CCDV-F lists objective 2.3 as messages, tools, streaming, vision, thinking, caching, third-party vendors (Bedrock/Vertex), Messages API data access patterns, Batch API, realtime vs batch tradeoffs. That's 6.8% of the exam, or three or four questions. They are usually short scenarios with a tell: "users stare at a blank screen", "the tool input fails to parse", "must stay in our AWS account", "reviewers must verify every claim", "the same 300-page manual in every request".
38b3f99ab7: Each feature in this chapter is the latest step of an older idea. Knowing the lineage makes the design choices obvious. It also tells you which experience from Java and telecom systems carries over.
f9f3490fe9:
HTTP/1.1 (1997 to 1999) added chunked transfer encoding, which lets a server start sending a response before it knows its length. Web developers then spent a decade pushing data to browsers with workarounds such as long polling and hidden iframes ("Comet").

The HTML5 work standardised two answers around 2009 to 2011. WebSockets is a full-duplex protocol that upgrades the connection away from HTTP. Server-Sent Events (the EventSource API and the text/event-stream format) is a one-way stream of named, text-framed events over an ordinary HTTP response.

SSE never became fashionable for browser apps. But it has properties an API provider wants:

  • it's plain HTTP, so it passes through corporate proxies, load balancers and API gateways that would break a websocket;
  • its wire format is trivial: event: and data: lines separated by a blank line;
  • it fits a request-response API where only the server has more to say.

When large language model APIs added streaming in 2020 to 2023, they all chose SSE for these reasons. Chapter 14 looks at the bytes on the wire. This chapter is about the events, and what your code does with them.
debc95ca16: For a telecom architect, the nearest relative is the progress notification in a long-running provisioning call. The northbound client gets "accepted", then a series of state-change events, then a final result. The lesson from those systems applies directly. The final status arrives last, and a client that acts on intermediate events must be ready for the final one to say something else.
78b6a6a5d0:
For decades, getting information out of a scanned form, a photo or a PDF meant a pipeline. OCR to text, then layout analysis, then template rules per document type, then a separate system to reason over the extracted fields. Every new form layout was a project.

Multimodal models replaced the middle of that pipeline. They encode images into the same representation as text, so the model reads a chart, a handwritten field note or a screenshot directly. Claude gained image input with the Claude 3 family in March 2024. PDF support followed in late 2024 as a beta. The API extracts the text of each page and also renders each page as an image, giving the model both (dates approximate; check the release notes).

That design choice, text plus image per page, is the key to everything section 09 says about PDF cost and quality.
0d66c73de5:
Retrieval-augmented generation was named in a 2020 paper by Lewis and colleagues. But the architecture is what search engineers had built for years: index documents, retrieve the relevant ones for a query, and present them with the answer. The new part was putting retrieved passages into a generative model's prompt.

The weakness was provenance. A model asked to "quote your sources" can paraphrase, merge or invent quotations. Anthropic's Citations feature (January 2025) made grounding structural. The API chunks your documents. The response carries machine-readable pointers to the exact spans the model relied on, with the cited text copied from your document rather than generated. Later, search-result blocks extended the same mechanism to results from your own retrieval pipeline.

In regulated industries, this is the difference between "the assistant says the lease allows it" and "the assistant cites clause 14.3 on page 22, which a reviewer can open".
221a778695:
Enterprise integration has a name for "don't put large payloads in messages; store them and pass a reference". It's the claim check pattern (Hohpe and Woolf, 2003). You've used it whenever a Kafka event carried an S3 key instead of a 20 MB document.

The Files API, introduced in beta in May 2025 and now generally available on the Claude API, is the claim check for the Messages API. Upload once, get a file_id, and reference it in any number of requests. Like every claim check, it saves transport and payload size. It doesn't make the consumer's work smaller. That's why the file's content is still billed as input tokens.
1f46bd5a2f:
Large enterprises buy software through their cloud providers. Procurement is already done, spending counts toward committed-use agreements, and identity and audit already work. Claude has been available on Amazon Bedrock since 2023 and on Google Cloud Vertex AI since 2024 (approximate; check the platform pages).

The platforms serve the same models with the same Messages request body. But each wraps it in its own authentication, endpoint and model naming scheme. And each adopts new Anthropic features on its own schedule. That last point, feature lag, is the one most likely to break a design, and the one the exam likes.
de73032e1a:
To see what streaming does and doesn't do, split the time of one Messages API call into its parts.

First there is network and queueing time. Then the model reads the whole prompt in one parallel pass, called prefill. Its cost grows with input length. That's why a 150,000-token prompt takes noticeably longer to start answering than a 2,000-token one (prompt caching, chapter 15, cuts it). Then the model generates output one token at a time, called decode. Each token needs a forward pass, so decode time grows linearly with output length.

A non-streaming call returns nothing until the last output token exists. A streaming call returns the first token as soon as it is decoded, and each later token as it appears.
1bb06a4c3b:
So streaming changes one number, time to first token (TTFT), and leaves the others alone. Total time to the last token is the same. The tokens generated are the same, so the cost is the same. The answer is the same.

What changes is what a human sees. Text starts appearing in well under a second, instead of after ten or twenty seconds of blank screen. In a chat UI, a copilot, a care agent's assist panel or an IDE, that difference decides whether the product feels responsive. In a backend job that parses a JSON object out of the response, it decides nothing. The code can't act until the object is complete anyway.
514a64fec6:
There's a second, less visible reason to stream: connection lifetime. A long generation (a 30,000-token report, a long extended-thinking run) can take minutes. A non-streamed HTTP request that sends nothing back for minutes looks idle to every proxy, NAT gateway and load balancer on the path. Many of them drop idle connections after 60 to 350 seconds. A stream keeps bytes moving: content deltas, and ping events when there's nothing else.

The SDKs know this. The streaming docs say streaming is especially useful for requests with large max_tokens values, "where the SDK requires streaming to avoid HTTP timeouts". The Python SDK refuses a non-streaming request it estimates will run too long, and tells you to stream. (The exact threshold is an SDK detail; check the docs.)
2caf8afa7b:
The companion example 06_ttft_vs_total.py turns this into arithmetic with a simulated clock: 0.6 seconds of prefill and 60 output tokens per second. At 600 output tokens, the streamed version shows text at 0.62 seconds and the non-streamed version at 10.6 seconds. Both finish at 10.6 seconds. At 40 tokens, a typical classification, the gain is 0.65 seconds, for a response that only code reads.

The point the exam wants you to hold is simple: streaming reduces perceived latency, not total latency, tokens or cost. An option that says "enable streaming to reduce cost" or "stream to make the batch job faster" is wrong.
1bb711ca03:
Set "stream": true on a Messages request (or use the SDK's stream helper), and the response becomes a sequence of Server-Sent Events. The grammar mirrors the structure of a normal response from chapter 05. A message contains an ordered list of content blocks, and each block has a type.

In the stream, the message is opened. Each block is opened, filled by deltas and closed. Then the message is closed with its stop reason and final usage. Once you see it as "open, fill, close" at two levels, every event makes sense.
65e5637bc5:
A few details in that table are worth slowing down for.

The index on block events is the position of the block in the final content list. It's how deltas find their buffer. Blocks are streamed one after another, but your code should key on the index rather than assume order.

The output token count in message_delta is cumulative (the docs are explicit about this). So you record it; you don't add it to a running total.

Thinking blocks (extended or adaptive thinking, chapter 13) stream as thinking_delta text followed by a signature_delta. The signature must be preserved when you send the block back in a later turn. That's one more reason to let the SDK accumulate.

The docs also describe a fallback block. It arrives as a start and stop pair with no deltas, when the server falls back during a response. Treat unknown block and delta types as "store and pass through", never as a crash (check the docs for its exact semantics).
3b388ff186: Here is a worked trace of a short response, printed the way example 02 of the companion prints events, with eight-character chunks. The user wrote "No internet in 07302", and the model decided to say one sentence and then call a tool:
172b4034b1: Three consequences follow from the grammar, and each has its own section. Tool input arrives as fragments of a JSON string (section 05). The stop reason arrives last (section 06). And an error can arrive after the HTTP status line said 200 (section 06).
ee34a5a15c: Your application logic wants a complete message: a list of finished content blocks, a stop reason and usage. So do the tool loop from chapter 02, the logging and the cost tracking. Streaming gives you the pieces. Accumulation is the step that rebuilds the message from events, and there are two ways to do it.
0207871820:
The Python and TypeScript SDKs provide a stream helper, client.messages.stream(...), used as a context manager. It exposes text_stream, an iterator over just the text deltas, already decoded to strings. It also exposes get_final_message(), which "collects all events into the complete Message object", including tool inputs parsed into dictionaries. You can also iterate the helper itself to see every event.

The helper is the right default. With it, the rest of your code becomes identical for streamed and non-streamed calls. You render text as it arrives, then hand the final message to the same loop.
aa1342963d: The test in that example checks the property that makes the helper trustworthy: the concatenated deltas equal the text of the final message. If you write your own accumulator, that's the first test to write too.
fd91dde9e0:
You drop to raw events (client.messages.create(..., stream=True) returns an iterator of event objects) when you need to react to specific events. Examples: showing a "checking your line..." indicator the moment a tool_use block opens, forwarding events unchanged to another service, or measuring TTFT exactly.

You also need to understand the raw events to debug anything, and the exam asks about them. The accumulator is a small state machine: a dictionary of buffers keyed by block index, with one branch per event type.
92455081a9:
Production accumulators also handle more cases:

  • thinking_delta and signature_delta: append to a thinking block, keep the signature;
  • citations_delta: append one citation to the current text block's list (section 11);
  • unknown types: keep, log, don't crash.

That growing list of cases is the practical argument for the SDK helper. Anthropic adds block types, and the helper learns them when you upgrade the SDK.
1d63abacd4:
The most common streaming bug is treating each input_json_delta as JSON. A fragment is a slice of a JSON string, cut wherever the generator happened to be: {"msisd, then n": "20, then 1555010. The first json.loads throws.

Worse variants don't throw. Code that tries to parse, catches the error and "uses what it has" will act on half an argument. So will a regex that pulls a value out of a partial string. For a tool like start_port_in, that's a request against the wrong number.
01796cd860: You may want to show tool arguments while they stream, for example a large file a coding tool is writing. Use a partial-JSON parser for display only. Still execute the tool only from the parse at block stop. The SDKs ship such helpers for display (check the docs for names in your language).
4468992911:
By default, the API buffers and validates each tool parameter value before streaming it. So a large parameter (a whole document or file body) shows nothing until it's complete.

Setting "eager_input_streaming": true on a tool definition turns on fine-grained tool streaming for that tool. Fragments arrive as soon as the model starts the parameter, without server-side buffering or JSON validation. The docs state the consequence directly: "you might receive partial or invalid JSON". And a response that ends with max_tokens can cut a parameter off midway.

The documented handling is to accumulate, guard the parse, and check the stop reason. If parsing fails, send the raw string back to the model as a tool_result with "is_error": true, wrapped as {"INVALID_JSON": "..."}. The per-tool field replaces an older beta header (fine-grained-tool-streaming-2025-05-14) that you may still see in older code.
68f2fb1a2c: A non-streamed call either succeeds with a complete response or fails with an HTTP error status. A stream has a third outcome. It starts successfully, then fails or ends in a way the user didn't expect, after some text is already on the screen. Three failure modes cover nearly all of it.
295dea30c6:
The HTTP status line is sent when the stream opens. If the service becomes overloaded halfway through generation, it can't change a 200 into a 529. It sends an error event instead. The docs give the example of an overloaded_error, "which would normally correspond to an HTTP 529 in a non-streaming context". The SDKs turn that event into an exception raised from the iterator.

Code that checks only the status code, or wraps the loop in a broad try/except: pass, ends up displaying a partial answer as if it were complete. For a billing explanation, a half sentence that stops before "promotional credit ended" is a wrong answer, not a short one.
691bdb3094:
Two design choices hide in that code.

First, a stream can't be resumed. There's no "continue from event 37". Recovery means a new request, and the retry and backoff policy from chapter 05 applies unchanged. (The SDKs retry connection-level failures automatically, but an error after content has been delivered is your decision.)

Second, the UI needs a state for "this text is still being generated" that is distinct from "this is the answer". Chat interfaces get this for free by showing a cursor. APIs that relay streams to other services must send an explicit final event with a status. The Spring example in section 07 does that.
fbbe1f912b:
The stop_reason is in message_delta, the second-to-last event. By the time you know why generation stopped, you've rendered everything. Two cases matter.

  • If the reason is max_tokens, the text was cut off. The UI should say so and offer to continue, with a follow-up request that has the partial answer in the history (chapter 05).
  • If the reason is tool_use, the text was a preamble ("Let me check your line"), and the real answer will come after a tool round. The UI should show a working state, not a finished answer.

Example 05 renders both, and asserts that the stop reason was seen within the last two events. The broken pattern is a UI that marks a message "done" when text stops arriving. It looks right in the demo, and wrong on the first long answer.
2ceb429a56:
When a browser tab closes or a mobile client loses signal, the downstream connection breaks. But your server's upstream stream to the API keeps running, and keeps generating billable tokens.

Close the upstream stream when the downstream client disconnects. In Python, leaving the with block closes it. In Java, close the StreamResponse. In Spring, register onCompletion and onTimeout callbacks on the emitter that cancel the upstream task. Tokens generated before cancellation are billed; tokens never generated are not.
6312afcce3:
In an enterprise application, the browser almost never talks to the Anthropic API directly. The API key (or cloud credential) must stay on the server. So the backend opens the upstream stream and relays a simplified stream to the client.

That relay is where you translate events into your own contract:

  • forward text deltas;
  • send a "tool started" event if the UI shows activity;
  • send a final event with the stop reason;
  • send an explicit error event if the upstream fails.

The client should never have to know Anthropic's event names.
d7fbe82ec0:
In Spring MVC, SseEmitter is the natural fit. In WebFlux, return a Flux<ServerSentEvent<String>>. Run the upstream stream off the request thread; a virtual-thread executor suits blocking I/O like this. And close upstream when the client leaves.

The Anthropic Java SDK exposes createStreaming, which returns a closeable stream of raw events. It also has a MessageAccumulator helper for building the final message. (Class names are per the Java SDK at the time of writing; check the docs for your version.)
96c7e22775: Streaming and the agent loop compose without changing the loop. Each turn is streamed for the user. The loop decides what to do from the accumulated final message, exactly as it would without streaming. The only addition is cosmetic: when a tool_use block opens, the UI can show which tool is running. Example 16 asserts that the loop needs four messages (question, tool call, tool result, answer) whether streamed or not.
14f33374c7:
Claude accepts images as image content blocks in user turns, including inside tool results. The model doesn't run OCR and then read the text. The API resizes the image if needed, cuts it into patches, and encodes them into the same representation the model uses for text tokens. Attention then runs over image and text together.

That's why it can answer "which port on this patch panel has no cable", read a handwritten field ticket, describe a chart, or compare a screenshot with a spec. It's also why images have a token cost and occupy the context window like text. Claude reads images; it doesn't generate them.
27c34d3b8d:
An image block has a source of one of three types.

  • base64 embeds the bytes in the request with a media_type. It works everywhere, and it's the only option on Bedrock and Vertex.
  • url points at a publicly reachable image that the API fetches. It keeps requests small, but it depends on the URL being reachable from Anthropic's side. It isn't supported on Bedrock or Vertex.
  • file references a file_id from the Files API (section 10).

Supported formats are JPEG, PNG, GIF and WebP. For animated GIFs, only the first frame is used.
7ae19113c2: The prompt layout in that example follows the documented guidance. Put images before the question. When there are several, introduce each with a short label ("Image 1: ...") and refer to the labels in the question. A model looking at three unlabelled photos has to guess which one "the installed cabinet" means.
9b315fab4e:
Work one example by hand. A 1092 x 1092 screenshot is within the caps, so it costs ceil(1092/28) x ceil(1092/28) = 39 x 39 = 1,521 visual tokens. That's about the same as 1,100 words of text.

A 4032 x 3024 phone photo is first scaled so the long edge is 1568 px. Then, because 56 x 42 patches would exceed the token cap, it's scaled further to roughly 1250 x 936, about 1,530 tokens. The 12 megapixels bought nothing the 1.2-megapixel version didn't. A field-service app that uploads full-resolution photos pays for it in mobile upload time and request latency, not in tokens.

The lesson for system design: resize on the client, to the size the model will see. Keep the limits in configuration, because they differ by model tier and platform.
500f9ea4f0:
The documented limitations are worth knowing, because exam distractors exploit them.

  • Claude won't identify real people from their faces.
  • It can be wrong on low-quality, rotated or very small images (under about 200 px).
  • Coordinates and spatial measurements are approximate. Don't ask it to measure a cable run from a photo and trust the centimetres.
  • Counts of many small objects are approximate.
  • It can't reliably tell whether an image is AI-generated.
  • It isn't designed to interpret diagnostic medical scans.

A design that depends on any of these as a hard guarantee needs a different tool or a human check.
5d3543efb3:
The most common vision anti-pattern is sending an image of something that already exists as text. Think of a screenshot of a table from your own database, a rendered PDF page of a contract you have in Word, or a photo of a configuration file. The image costs more tokens than the text. It loses exactness (a 0 read as an O). And it can't be cited at character level.

Send the data as text, or as a document with citations. Use vision for content that only exists visually: field photos, scanned forms, whiteboard sketches, screenshots of a third-party UI you can't query, charts in a slide deck.
a2a715f59f:
A PDF goes in a document content block. The mechanism explains both its cost and its strength. For each page, the API extracts the text and also converts the page into an image. The model receives both; the docs describe it as "a combination of text and images for analysis".

So the model can use the text layer for exact wording, and the page image for layout. Think of a table whose meaning depends on column alignment, a chart, a signature block, a stamped "VOID".

The price is that every page costs its text tokens plus its image tokens. The docs estimate 1,500 to 3,000 text tokens per page, depending on density, plus image costs computed as in section 08. A 40-page lease is on the order of 100,000 to 200,000 input tokens.
b480aa9200: Sources mirror images: base64, url (a PDF hosted online) and file (a Files API file_id). Plain text can also be sent as a document, with source.type "text" and media_type "text/plain". That's the usual way to make text citable. A third document form, custom content, takes a list of text blocks you've already chunked. Section 11 explains why you'd want that.
c12b3810e7:
Practical rules follow from the mechanism.

  • Put the document before the question, as with images.
  • For long documents, ask the model to find and quote the relevant passages first, then answer from them. It improves accuracy on long inputs (chapter 17).
  • If you'll ask several questions about the same document, put cache_control on the document block. Later questions then read it from the cache at a fraction of the input price (chapter 15).
  • If a document exceeds the page limit, split it by page ranges. Or extract the text yourself and send only the relevant sections.

Example 08 runs a pre-flight check of pages and payload size, and plans the split.
185253b4e1:
Amazon Bedrock offers two APIs for Claude. InvokeModel takes the Anthropic request body. The Bedrock Converse API is a provider-neutral format.

In Converse, full visual PDF understanding (text plus page images) requires citations to be enabled. Without them, Converse falls back to text extraction only. The docs give a 3-page example as roughly 1,000 tokens in text-only mode and 7,000 with full visual analysis. If a Bedrock team reports that "Claude cannot see the charts in our PDFs", this is the first thing to check.
acc601fadf:
Base64 inlining sends the whole file in every request. Ask five questions about a 20 MB lease, and you upload 27 MB of base64 five times. Each request is close to the size limit, and each pays upload time over the network.

The Files API separates storage from use. You upload a file once with POST /v1/files and receive a file_id. Any message can then include a block whose source is {"type": "file", "file_id": ...}. It's the claim-check pattern: the message carries the claim, and the store holds the payload.
7bafa73412:
The Files API is now generally available on the Claude API and needs no beta header. Older code sends anthropic-beta: files-api-2025-04-14, which still works. Depending on your SDK version, the methods may live under client.beta.files or client.files (check the docs for your SDK). The endpoints are:

  • upload: POST /v1/files
  • list: GET /v1/files
  • metadata: GET /v1/files/{file_id}
  • download: GET /v1/files/{file_id}/content
  • delete: DELETE /v1/files/{file_id}
a0df384740:
Here's a common story. A team builds a lease assistant on the direct API with uploaded file_ids. Then the security review moves production to Bedrock. Every request now fails with a 400, because neither the file source nor URL sources exist there.

The fix isn't a rewrite. It's a capability check with a fallback, decided once in the client layer. On platforms without the Files API, send base64 and mark the document for caching, so repeat questions stay cheap. Example 15 runs both versions against all three platforms.
98c312e3a6: Retention deserves its own word for this reader. A file you upload is a copy of customer or contract data, held by a processor until you delete it. In a telecom context with CPNI and privacy obligations, uploads must be registered in the same data inventory as any other store, with deletion wired into the retention job. Example 09 runs that job against a fake store and asserts that nothing is left.
59cc4d2f13:
An answer about a lease, a tariff or a regulatory filing is only useful if a reviewer can check it. Prompting for quotes ("cite the clause you rely on") helps. But the quote is generated text. It can be paraphrased, merged from two places, or invented, and your code can't tell which.

The Citations feature changes where the quote comes from. You set "citations": {"enabled": true} on each document block. The API chunks the documents (by sentence for plain text and PDFs), and the model answers. The response text is split into several text blocks, and those that rely on a source carry a citations list. Each citation includes cited_text, copied from your document rather than generated, plus a location you can map back to the source.
84830258a3:
Every citation also carries document_index (0-indexed across all document blocks in the request, across all messages) and document_title. The title and context fields on a document are passed to the model, but they aren't citable. context is a good place for metadata such as site ID and effective date.

On cost, the docs make two points. Enabling citations slightly increases input tokens (system prompt additions and chunking). And cited_text doesn't count toward output tokens, nor toward input tokens when passed back in later turns.
38197aa6da: Not with structured outputs. Enabling citations on any document or search-result block together with the structured-output format parameter (output_config.format) returns a 400. If you need both JSON and provenance, ask for citations and build the JSON in code from the cited blocks. Or use a tool schema that includes quote fields (check the docs for the current position).
f7e50da1d4: Text only. Image citations aren't supported. So a scanned PDF with no extractable text can't be cited, even though the model can read it.
140cc715f8: Granularity. Plain text and PDFs are cited at sentence level. If you need clause-level citations (one per contract clause, one per KB section), send custom content or search-result blocks chunked the way you want.
fb23914215: Works with prompt caching (cache the document block; citation blocks themselves aren't cached), token counting and batch processing. It's available on the Claude API, Bedrock and Vertex.
fa7c4cd6b2:
When you stream a cited answer, citations arrive as content_block_delta events whose delta type is citations_delta. Each carries one citation to append to the current text block's list.

An accumulator that ignores unknown delta types silently loses all provenance. It's a quiet failure, because the answers still look fine. A test that asserts the number of citations survives streaming catches it. (The companion's fake stream emits citations_delta.)
e153f5af81:
When your own retrieval returns passages, you can pass them as search_result blocks rather than as plain text. Each has a source (any stable string: a URL, or an ID like kb://art-2207), a title, a content list of text blocks, and an optional citations flag.

They can appear in user messages and inside tool results, so a search_kb tool can return them directly. If a tool result contains any search-result block, all of its blocks must be search results. The answer then cites search_result_locations with your source IDs, which your UI can turn into links to the knowledge-base article. No beta header is needed.
14a7e3fc07: Say a scenario requires that reviewers, auditors or customers can verify the source of each claim. The API-level answer is citations on documents (or search-result blocks for RAG), not a prompt instruction to include quotes. The prompt version produces text that looks like a quote. The feature produces a pointer your code can check.
fdf639c1d8:
The model knows nothing about your customers, your inventory, your network topology or this morning's outage. And the Messages API keeps no state between calls (chapter 05). So every request must carry whatever the model needs, or give it a way to get it.

That one constraint produces three basic patterns, which the exam calls Messages API data-access patterns. They differ in who chooses the data and when.
c04cac6f72: Stuffing (context loading). Your code puts the whole relevant data set into the prompt: a policy document, a product catalogue, a customer's full case history. Your code chooses, before the call, and it chooses everything.
cce15e514c: Retrieval (RAG). Your code searches an index with the user's question and puts the top results into the prompt. Your code chooses, before the call, but only the part that looks relevant.
52241be5c0: Tools. The model gets functions such as get_account or search_kb, and decides during the conversation what to fetch. The model chooses, at run time, as many times as it needs.
9f452f8dee:
Three supporting mechanisms are variations rather than new patterns:

  • an MCP server packages tools (and resources) so many applications can share one implementation (chapter 22);
  • the Files API is a transport optimisation for stuffing;
  • server tools such as web search and web fetch are tools that Anthropic runs for you against public data.
77563dc22c:
Stuffing is the simplest pattern, and often the best one. It has no retrieval step that can miss. The model sees everything and can connect facts across the document. And with prompt caching, a stable document set becomes cheap to resend: cached reads cost a small fraction of the base input price (chapter 15).

Its limits are size and attention. A corpus larger than the window can't be stuffed at all. Even inside a 1M-token window, cost and latency grow with every token. And recall of one specific fact buried in a very long context is less reliable than recall from a short one.

It also fails for data that changes per user or per minute. The stuffed copy is stale, or wrong for the next caller.
2ae10f4515:
Retrieval scales to corpora of any size and keeps each prompt small. But it adds a system: a chunking and indexing pipeline, and an embedding model or search engine. It also adds a new failure mode, the retrieval miss. If the right passage isn't in the top results, the model answers from what it got, confidently. RAG quality is mostly retrieval quality.

Retrieval also fragments context. A question whose answer needs two passages from different documents depends on both being retrieved.
21d3b89045:
Tools fit data that lives in systems of record and differs per user: balances, orders, tickets, outage status. They are the only pattern that gives fresh data and can enforce authorisation per call.

They cost round trips, since each tool call is another model turn (chapter 02). And the model must choose well, which depends on tool descriptions (chapter 21). A tool that wraps a search index is "agentic retrieval". The model can reformulate and search again, at the price of more turns.
7b850893ae:
Example 13 makes the trade-off concrete. It uses placeholder prices (3 dollars per million input tokens and 15 per million output, 1.25x for cache writes and 0.1x for cache reads; check current pricing) and 300,000 requests a month.

  • A 20,000-token policy stuffed without caching costs about 19,500 dollars a month.
  • With caching, assuming about 9,000 cache writes as the cache expires and refills, it costs about 3,950.
  • RAG with five 600-token chunks and 400 dollars of index infrastructure costs about 4,630.

For a 150,000-token corpus, stuffing costs about 136,500 uncached and 19,700 cached, while RAG stays at 4,630.

The shape of the result matters more than the numbers: for small, stable, heavily reused documents, stuffing with caching is competitive with RAG and simpler; as the corpus grows, retrieval wins on cost by a widening margin.
61bb0ab66f:
Real systems combine them. Take a carrier's care assistant. It might:

  • stuff and cache the 40-page plan catalogue and the conduct policy, which are small, stable and needed on every turn;
  • retrieve from 30,000 knowledge-base articles with search-result blocks, so answers cite article IDs;
  • call get_account, get_line_usage and get_outage_status tools against live systems, with the caller's identity propagated for authorisation;
  • get those tools from an MCP server that the retail-store assistant and the internal Claude Code setup also use.

Each data source sits in the pattern that matches its size, freshness and ownership.
0dc1fad422:
The first mismatch is stuffing data that should be fetched. A team puts a nightly export of each customer's last 200 orders into the system prompt, "so the model always has context". The export is stale by mid-morning, and the prompt is large on every turn. And when the export job mixes up two accounts, the model leaks one customer's orders to another.

The fix is a tool that fetches the current orders for the authenticated caller only. Authorisation is enforced in the tool, not in the prompt.
ef392c1b4a: The second mismatch is the reverse: building a vector index for a 20-page returns policy. The index adds a pipeline, an embedding bill and retrieval misses. (The policy's exception clause is in chunk 31, which never ranks in the top five.) All that to save tokens that caching would have saved anyway. Stuff it, cache it, and spend the engineering time elsewhere.
3d7dfa5560:
Why would a team use Claude through Bedrock instead of directly? Not for a different model; the models are the same. The reasons are organisational, and for a large carrier they are often decisive.

  • Authentication uses AWS IAM, so there's no new class of long-lived secret to manage. A pod's IAM role is the credential.
  • Spending lands on the AWS bill and counts toward existing commitments, and procurement is already done.
  • Traffic can stay on private networking within the AWS estate (check the docs for current private-connectivity options).
  • Logs and audit go to CloudTrail and CloudWatch, which the security team already watches.
  • Regional inference profiles support data-residency requirements.

If a scenario says "the company standardises on AWS and requires traffic and billing to stay in its AWS account", the answer is Bedrock.
d072a41967:
Very little. The Python SDK ships a platform client, AnthropicBedrock, installed with pip install -U "anthropic[bedrock]". It takes the same messages.create call with the same body.

Authentication has three routes:

  • the default AWS credential chain (environment variables, ~/.aws/credentials, an instance or pod role);
  • explicit aws_access_key, aws_secret_key and aws_session_token;
  • a Bedrock API key, passed as api_key or via AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK.

The region comes from aws_region or AWS_REGION. If none resolves, the client raises an error.
a8b39c7995:
Bedrock names models differently. A base model ID looks like anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929-v1:0: provider prefix, model name, date, version suffix. Newer IDs drop some of those parts (for example anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6).

AWS serves newer Claude models through cross-region inference. For those, a request with the bare base ID fails with a 400. You must use an inference profile ID, which adds a geographic prefix such as global., us., eu., jp. or apac., or a full inference-profile ARN.

Global profiles route anywhere, for maximum availability. Regional profiles keep traffic within a geography for data residency. Per the docs, they carry a 10% price premium over global for Sonnet 4.5 and later models.

The exact IDs for the newest models change with each release. Look them up in the Bedrock model catalog, and keep them in configuration, never in code.
a5af6d8753:
InvokeModel (and its streaming variant) takes the Anthropic Messages body. It's what AnthropicBedrock uses, and it gives the fullest feature set.

Converse is Bedrock's provider-neutral chat API. It's convenient if you switch between vendors' models. But it has its own request shape, and some Claude behaviours differ, such as the PDF citations requirement in section 09.

When a scenario asks for maximum Claude feature support on Bedrock, InvokeModel is the answer.
048b0ab804:
The Bedrock page lists features that are not supported. At the time of writing that includes:

  • URL sources for images and documents, and the Files API;
  • the server-side tools code execution, web search and web fetch;
  • Agent Skills, the MCP connector and programmatic tool calling;
  • the Message Batches, Models, Admin and Usage endpoints;
  • Claude Managed Agents;
  • server-side fallback;
  • the top-level automatic prompt-caching field (explicit cache_control breakpoints still work).

Bedrock has its own batch inference service, which is a different API from Anthropic's Message Batches (check the AWS docs). Beta features are enabled in the request body (an anthropic_beta array) rather than through a header.

The list moves. So the durable lesson is the habit: check the platform's feature page before designing around a feature.
114c9534dd:
The Vertex story is the same, with Google's nouns. A team that runs on Google Cloud gets IAM-based authentication, GCP billing and commitments, VPC Service Controls and Cloud Audit Logs.

The SDK client is AnthropicVertex (pip install -U "anthropic[vertex]"), and it takes a project_id and a region. Authentication uses Google Application Default Credentials. Locally that's gcloud auth application-default login; in production, a service account or workload identity.
8137cf7e1e:
Three details differ on the wire. The SDK client handles all of them, but they're worth knowing for raw HTTP or debugging.

  • The model isn't in the request body. It's part of the Vertex endpoint URL.
  • The API version goes in the body as anthropic_version with the value vertex-2023-10-16, not in a header.
  • Model IDs use Vertex's format. Older models append @date (claude-haiku-4-5@20251001). Newer ones use the bare name (for example claude-opus-5-5).
bced85ae0d:
Endpoints come in three kinds.

  • The global endpoint is recommended for availability and has no premium, but it supports only pay-as-you-go traffic.
  • Multi-region endpoints (us, eu) keep traffic within a geography.
  • Regional endpoints (such as us-east5) are needed for single-region data residency or provisioned throughput.

Multi-region and regional endpoints carry a 10% premium for newer models. The docs note that specific regional endpoints support only some models, with the newest served from global or multi-region endpoints (check the docs for your model).

Unsupported features on Vertex at the time of writing include URL sources and the Files API, the code execution and web fetch server tools, Agent Skills, the MCP connector, and programmatic tool calling. The Message Batches endpoint is also missing (Vertex has its own batch prediction; check the Google docs), as are Claude Managed Agents. Request payloads are limited to 30 MB.
be9dac8e9b:
Put sections 13 and 14 side by side, and a pattern appears.

  • The body is portable: messages, system prompt, content blocks, tools, tool_choice, thinking, citations, explicit cache breakpoints.
  • The envelope is not: authentication, endpoint, model ID, region, quotas, billing, logs.
  • The feature set lags. New features and betas usually reach the direct Claude API first and the cloud platforms later, some never. Storage-backed or Anthropic-run features (Files API, URL fetching, server tools, batches, managed agents) are the most likely to be missing.
a51395c5ec:
For a Spring shop the shape is familiar:

  • a @Configuration class with a @ConditionalOnProperty("claude.platform") bean per platform;
  • model IDs in application-{profile}.yml;
  • a ClaudeCapabilities bean that services query before using a platform-specific feature.

The Anthropic Java SDK has Bedrock and Vertex backends configured on the client builder (check the Java SDK docs for the exact class names). So the rest of the code keeps using the same AnthropicClient interface.

Claude Code and the Agent SDK can also be pointed at Bedrock or Vertex with environment variables (CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK=1, CLAUDE_CODE_USE_VERTEX=1; check the docs). That matters when an enterprise allows developer tools only through its cloud account (chapter 10 covers model pinning).
19fb350d3e: CCDV-F items on this material are short scenarios with four options. The wrong options are usually real features applied to the wrong problem: streaming offered as a cost fix, the Files API offered as a token fix, vision offered where text exists, a prompt instruction offered where a feature guarantees the property. Work each one before reading the reasoning.
60a4af00bc:
The problem is perceived latency on a long output that a person is watching. That's exactly what streaming fixes: time to first token drops to roughly the prefill time, while total time and cost stay the same.

A breaks the interactive use case: Batch has no latency guarantee, and drafts depend on the live conversation. C truncates answers, producing max_tokens stops. D doesn't change decode speed.
21557e8484:
Each input_json_delta is a fragment of a JSON string, not a JSON value. Only the concatenation is valid, and it's complete at content_block_stop. B is the documented handling, and the SDK helper does it for you.

A misunderstands the transport: the model already produces valid JSON, and the stream splits it. C throws away streaming for no reason. D acts on half an argument, which for a real tool means a wrong action.
c55b30528c:
The AWS constraint selects Bedrock. "Verify the clause and page" selects citations on document blocks, which return page_location with exact cited_text. On Bedrock, PDFs must be base64 (no Files API, no URL sources), and caching cuts the cost of repeat questions.

A violates the AWS policy and relies on generated quotes. C duplicates what PDF support already does (text plus page image), and it loses citations, which work only on extractable text. D designs around a feature Bedrock doesn't have.
a5a3253bc1:
The Files API saves bytes on the wire. File content is still billed as input tokens on every request that references it. Prompt caching is the mechanism that cuts the cost of a large, stable prefix resent many times (chapter 15).

For a 300-page manual used by every request, retrieval (section 12) may be a better long-term design. But of the options, B addresses the cost. A is the misconception the scenario tests. C does nothing for tokens. D changes latency perception, not cost.
9771ef54d0: Live, frequently changing data from a system of record calls for tools. Reuse across several applications and agents is the tell for an MCP server (this is official sample question 3). One server gives one implementation, one place for authorisation and one place to fix bugs. A and D are stale and oversized. B is the wrong pattern for exact, current, structured data such as stock counts.
8c5c9144ef:
Errors can arrive after the 200, because the status line is sent when the stream opens. And stop_reason arrives last. So both must be handled after text is rendered. B handles both with the documented signals.

A checks the wrong thing. Raising max_tokens reduces truncation, but it doesn't detect it. C fixes error visibility by giving up streaming's benefit. D parses natural language to detect a condition the API reports structurally.
88e153ef0a: Live: send the same 600-token prompt with and without streaming, and record TTFT and total time. Send a full-resolution phone photo and a client-resized one, and compare usage.input_tokens. Upload a PDF with the Files API, ask three cited questions, then delete the file.
77da15679c: Done when: you can draw the event sequence from memory, and say which event carries the stop reason and why tool JSON is parsed at block stop. You can compute image tokens for a given size. You can state what the Files API saves and what it doesn't. And you can pick stuffing, retrieval or tools for a data source in one sentence, and Bedrock, Vertex or direct for a platform constraint in another.
